clinicalPearls: Contact urticaria is an immediate wheal-and-flare reaction appearing within minutes of skin contact with a triggering substance, unlike the delayed pattern of allergic contact dermatitis
It is divided into non-immunological reactions (direct release of mediators, for example from certain foods, plants or chemicals) and immunological IgE-mediated reactions in sensitised individuals
Natural rubber latex is a classic occupational cause, notably in healthcare and among workers using latex gloves
Food handlers, bakers, farmers, hairdressers and healthcare staff are commonly affected occupational groups
Immunological contact urticaria can progress to generalised urticaria, angioedema, respiratory symptoms and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis
The hands are the usual site of occupational reactions, and symptoms typically settle when contact ends
Diagnosis is supported by the history and by cautious skin testing or specific IgE, with provocation testing done carefully because of the anaphylaxis risk
Management centres on identifying and avoiding the trigger, using substitutes such as non-latex gloves, and having a plan for systemic reactions
reference.pathophysiology: In the immunological form, prior sensitisation leads to allergen-specific IgE on mast cells; re-exposure cross-links IgE and triggers rapid mast cell degranulation with histamine release, producing the immediate wheal and flare and, if extensive, systemic effects. In the non-immunological form, substances act directly to release vasoactive mediators without prior sensitisation, generally causing localised reactions.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed occupational and exposure history with symptom timing
Skin prick testing to suspected agents such as latex, performed with resuscitation available
Open or use provocation tests done cautiously
Specific IgE blood testing where available
Assessment for coexisting asthma or rhinitis, especially with latex
redFlags: Progression to angioedema, wheeze or anaphylaxis requiring emergency treatment
Widespread reaction beyond the site of contact
History of previous severe systemic reaction on re-exposure
reference.prognosis: Symptoms usually resolve once the causative contact is avoided, and the outlook is good with effective avoidance; however, sensitised individuals remain at risk of severe reactions on re-exposure, and latex allergy in particular can have systemic consequences.
pitfalls: Confusing immediate contact urticaria with delayed allergic contact dermatitis and choosing the wrong test
Performing provocation testing without resuscitation facilities in a potentially anaphylactic patient
Failing to recognise latex as a cause and continuing latex glove use
Not providing an emergency plan for those at risk of systemic reactions
management: Identify and avoid the causative substance, providing a latex-free environment where natural rubber latex is implicated
Prescribe an adrenaline auto-injector and an emergency action plan for individuals at risk of systemic reactions or anaphylaxis
Institute occupational measures such as substituting latex gloves and modifying the workplace for affected food handlers, healthcare and other at-risk workers
Assess and manage coexisting asthma and rhinitis, particularly with latex sensitisation
Confirm sensitisation with skin-prick or specific IgE testing performed with resuscitation facilities available, and counsel on the ongoing risk of severe reactions on re-exposure
